                    ### Question
                    A 32-year-old woman comes to her doctor’s office with abdominal distention, diffuse abdominal pain, and a history of 10–12 bowel movements a day for the last week. She was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease 3 years ago. Today, vitals are normal. Her abdomen is mildly distended and diffusely tender to palpation. A CT scan shows evidence of a fistula and strictures located in the last 30 cm of her ileum. A resection of the affected portion of the bowel is scheduled. What changes in bile metabolism are expected in this patient post-procedure?

                    ### Options

opb. Synthesis of cholesterol in the liver will decrease
opc. The balance of the components in bile will be altered
opd. Enteric bacteria will remain the same in the small intestine
ope. Absorption of  7⍺-dehydroxylated bile will decrease

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Following the resection of the ileum in a patient with Crohn's disease, significant changes in bile metabolism are expected due to the critical role of the terminal ileum in bile acid absorption. The removal of this section leads to decreased reabsorption of bile acids, which in turn disrupts the enterohepatic circulation. This disruption prompts the liver to increase bile acid synthesis to compensate, ultimately altering the balance of bile components. Additionally, the reduced reabsorption of bile acids can lead to an increased synthesis of bile acids from cholesterol, thereby potentially decreasing the liver's cholesterol levels. The evidence paths regarding Vitamin K and changes in intestinal bacteria, while correct, do not directly support the reasoning for changes in bile metabolism post-ileum resection and are thus less relevant to the specific question of bile metabolism changes.
